events.title: Spanish colonial rule
hints: Galleons from Acapulco stopped here for supplies for more than two centuries.
A mission established in 1668 led to wars with the indigenous population.
It was ceded after the war of 1898 while its neighbours were sold elsewhere.
events.summary: Spain established a mission in 1668, and war and disease reduced the Chamorro population sharply. The island became a stopover for Manila galleons and the administrative centre of the Marianas until it was ceded to the United States after the Spanish-American War in 1898.

events.title: US naval government
hints: A naval captain governed the island from 1899.
Residents were not citizens and could not elect a legislature with real powers.
The Organic Act of 1950 transferred control to civilians.
events.summary: From 1899 to 1950 the US Navy governed Guam through naval governors, using it as a coaling station and base. The Chamorro people were classified as nationals without citizenship until the Organic Act of 1950 granted citizenship and civilian government.

events.title: Japanese occupation
hints: Japan took the island days after the Pearl Harbor attack.
Residents were forced into labour and marches to camps.
US forces recaptured it in July and August 1944.
events.summary: Japan captured the island on 10 December 1941 and held it for about two and a half years. The Chamorro people were forced into labour, subject to violence and, in 1944, marched to concentration camps such as Manenggon. More than a thousand died before the US retook the island.
